book: 181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone

chapters.file: ch03 - The Blackwell Philosophy and Pop Culture Series.md
ch06 - Part Five D Is for Destiny.md
chapters.relation: The editor's introduction retells her childhood memory of being left behind at a Wisconsin carnival, narrated in Lost-style 'flashback' and 'flash-sideways' segments, to argue that the show grips everyone because it stages the universal fear of being cut off from all we know and love. She calls this a philosophical fear that forces the questions 'Why am I here? Does my life matter?' and then previews the volume's five parts: time travel metaphysics (Fortune), epistemology (Origin), social and political philosophy (Unity), ethics (Necessity), and religion (Destiny).

chapters.file: ch07 - PART ONE - F IS FOR FORTUNE.md

chapters.relation: Davies defends Lost's convoluted plotting using Aristotle's Poetics, arguing the show works as a tragicomic epic that keeps closure and relevance even with Juliet's pre-crash storyline, genre mixing (Hurley's golf course beside Sayid's captivity), and shifting characters like Ben. He then uses the 'We have to go back' flash-forward to lay out McTaggart's two conceptions of time, eternalism versus presentism, and argues the flash-forward pushes viewers toward fatalism about Jack's already-fixed meeting with Kate near LAX. Finally he contends the past cannot be changed - Hurley in 2007 cannot undo his 1977 stay in the Dharma Initiative, since contradictions would entail everything - so viewers enjoy the time-travel plot by 'shielding' its mutually contradictory time lines.

chapters.file: ch09 - None of It Matters Anyway, Then, Does It.md
chapters.relation: Devlin applies David Lewis's analysis of time travel (external versus personal time) to seasons 5 and 6: Faraday's 'whatever happened, happened' expresses an eternalist four-dimensional block universe in which Sayid's shooting of young Ben and Faraday's death at Eloise's hands were always part of the past. He reads the flash-sideways as initially exploring a branching-universe model in which Jughead's detonation actualizes an alternative 2004 time line. Lewis's tools then dissolve the puzzles: the Hurley-Miles 'we already had this conversation' exchange, baby and adult Miles as one person spread like a time-worm, the Faraday-kills-Eloise grandfather paradox, and the Locke-Richard compass causal loop, whose point of origin the show leaves unresolved.

Pierce argues that Lost's time travel runs on a fixed-time model in which nothing that happened can be undone, so the live question is ethical: Kate insists saving young Ben is still obligatory and Sayid remains responsible for shooting him, while Jack's plan to detonate Jughead at the Swan shows that trying to change the past can cause the very evil it targets, the Incident. Using Carneades' distinction between truth and necessity - future-tense truths made true by our own free choices - he shows that 'whatever happened, happened' does not abolish moral responsibility, applying the point to the Man in Black's causal-loop manipulation of Locke, Richard, and Ben. Desmond's consciousness travel in 'The Constant' is treated as the exception requiring hyper-time or alternate realities, and Pierce concludes that morality in time travel is simply ordinary morality, with Kate offering the most balanced view of the characters' choices.

Barnbaum treats the season 6 flash-sideways as counterfactual conditionals and evaluates them with David Lewis's possible-worlds semantics: in the closest possible world where James Ford's parents were still conned but he never became a grifter, Sawyer plausibly becomes a cop, whereas a world in which Jack fathers a child with Juliet demands too many extra changes to count as close to ours. She pairs this with Rawls's veil of ignorance - applied to dividing the crash survivors' water, where Jack's life-saving skill could justify unequal shares - as another famous hypothetical thought experiment whose conclusion rests on what people would agree to in the Original Position.

chapters.file: ch12 - PART TWO - O IS FOR ORIGIN.md

chapters.relation: Taliaferro and Kastrul ask what the reader would do in the castaways' place, using Aristotle's view that character is a disposition to act under other conditions to assess Mr. Eko, Ben, Michael, Charlie, and Sawyer: people are not merely what they do but what they would do. Plato's Ring of Gyges, quoted at length, tests whether characters like Sun behave honestly only when watched. Against the idea that the island could reverse all values, they argue morality cannot be completely relative to context - invoking Chesterton's 'Thou shalt not steal' on the remotest star - and place Lost in the island-narrative tradition of the Odyssey and Robinson Crusoe as a story of the journey of the soul.

Addey analyzes the show's web of coincidences - Sawyer and Boone crossing paths in the Australian police station, Jack meeting Desmond in the hatch - and distinguishes genuine coincidence from divine providence, fatalism, and determinism. She applies Jung's theory of synchronicity to Locke's walkabout conviction that he was 'meant' to reach the island, then uses the birthday paradox, the law of truly large numbers, confirmation bias, and Popper's falsifiability to show why viewers and conspiracy theorists overestimate the improbability of such connections. Finally she evaluates Jacob's candidacy experiment as flawed social science: the candidates' circumstantial ignorance, maintained by the Others' deceptions, undermines the free and morally responsible choices Jacob claims to be testing, which is why the curious Hurley deserved to become protector.

Barris argues Lost fascinates because it dramatizes the basic structures of life itself: the castaways are Heideggerian thrown into an island none of them chose, brought there by Desmond's lapse at the Swan and by interlocking backstories such as Sawyer's bar conversation with Jack's father. Against the existentialist claim (Sartre, Camus) that life is simply absurd, he uses Wittgenstein's On Certainty - doubting everything presupposes certainties - to argue life is a riddle of partial sense, which is why the show's connections between Hurley and Libby or Jack and Desmond always hint at meaning without resolving it. The finale answers only the question of life after death, leaving life after birth as open as our own.

Lee reads Jack, Locke, and Desmond as studies in Sartrean bad faith and authenticity: Christian Shephard's Red Sox fatalism is determinism as an excuse for moral failure, Locke swings from a Kierkegaardian leap of faith (pushing the button as his Abraham-and-Isaac trial) into nihilism when the Pearl film suggests the button is a psychological experiment, and Desmond's Humean skepticism yields to sacrificial faith in the fail-safe. He argues Jacob is the show's greatest con man, so Jack's acceptance of destiny in 'The End' remains a free choice rather than predestination. The finale's sideways world then moves Lost from secular existentialism to religious existentialism, read through Buber's I-Thou relation in Sawyer and Juliet's 'It worked' reunion and the all-religions church, where as Gandhi held every path leads to the same place.

chapters.file: ch17 - PART THREE - U IS FOR UNITY.md

chapters.relation: Davies treats the beach camp as an actual state of nature: the stolen drinking water is a tragedy of the commons, Shannon's inhalers show how the crash scrubs pre-existing property rights (Hobbes: two men desiring the same thing become enemies), and Jack and Sayid's torture of Sawyer marks the first step toward Locke's civil society by enforcing others' rights through punishment rather than self-defense. He rejects theories of human nature - Rousseauan 'Innocence' versus a 'Trust No One' outlook - in favor of the repeated prisoner's dilemma, arguing the survivors stabilize cooperation through tit-for-tat: beginning cooperative with strangers and retaliating against the Others. On this reading the real difference between Hobbes and Locke is which round of the repeated dilemma each takes as the starting point.

Fosl argues that although the survivors' internal order looks Lockean - Jack's uncoerced leadership, natural rights, minimal government - and is bonded by Rousseauan pity and Humean sympathy (Kate staying in the cage with Sawyer, 'live together, die alone'), the show's deepest political logic follows Carl Schmitt's friend-enemy distinction: the survivors cohere only in opposition to the Others, torture is excused in liberal terms, and conflicts end in redemptive violence, with Jack both killing the enemy and dying a Christlike sacrifice. Hobbes's absence from the character names signals the show's rejection of a war of all against all among the survivors, yet the finale's divine manipulation of the castaways, with Jacob treating people as means against Kantian autonomy, repudiates the liberal hope of a rational peace altogether.

holes.name: Aristotle's Poetics (tragedy, epic, and plot unity)
holes.what: Aristotle's account in the Poetics of tragedy and epic plot, including unity of action, closure, relevance, and rules about character, place, and time.
holes.why: Chapter 8's first half defends Lost's complicated storytelling by testing it against the Poetics' principles of closure, relevance, and unity, and the taxonomy has no concept covering narrative theory.

holes.name: Synchronicity (meaningful coincidence)
holes.what: Jung's principle that some coincidences are meaningful, acausal concurrences between inner psychic states and external events.
holes.why: Chapter 14's central analysis of Locke's walkabout and the castaways' intersections rests on Jung's theory of synchronicity, which the taxonomy lacks (only the collective unconscious is listed).

holes.name: The Prisoner's Dilemma and Tit-for-Tat
holes.what: A game-theory model in which rational self-interest blocks cooperation, with tit-for-tat reciprocity as the winning strategy when the game is repeated.
holes.why: Chapter 18 explains how the castaways build trust from scratch and reframes the Hobbes-Locke disagreement through repeated prisoner's dilemmas resolved by tit-for-tat, a framework absent from the taxonomy.

holes.name: The Tragedy of the Commons
holes.what: A situation in which individually rational use of a shared, dwindling resource destroys it, although collective restraint would preserve it for all.
holes.why: Chapter 18 analyzes the stolen drinking-water crisis on the beach as a tragedy of the commons requiring a rationing the survivors have no authority to enforce.

holes.name: Carl Schmitt
holes.what: German jurist and Nazi-era political theorist whose Concept of the Political defines politics by the friend-enemy distinction and treats conflict as inescapable rather than soluble.
holes.why: Chapter 19 is built around Schmitt: it argues the survivors' relation to the Others embodies his friend-enemy logic rather than liberal consensus politics, and the taxonomy has no entry for him.
